review_text_raw:
I don't know what qualities I should look for when reviewing horror games, but as someone who has been keen on horror games since childhood, I really enjoyed the game.
Jump-scares are unexpected and frightening, but it was the distorted faces and voices in the glitched videos that really struck me as "scary."

As for the points I don't like:
•Acting sucks. There were scenes that I cringed a lot while watching. Even the text messages are cringe... Like, there are literally missing people out there, and yet everyone uses weird emojis in every damn message.
•As someone who loves choice-based games, only a few of your choices affect the ending, and the game has only 4 different endings (which is way less than I expected.)
•I don't want to spoil the endings, but I must say, I didn't like any of them.
•The phone interface is not good. Its functionality is pretty limited. Chatting is slow, you can't switch between tabs; you can't use the tab button on the keyboard to switch between text boxes, and you can't start videos from a certain timestamp.

Other than these, it's definitely a fun and spooky experience. The price is totally acceptable for 5 hours (and multiple playthroughs with a new game+ / fast chatting mode), so I recommend it.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

This is a decent "choices matter" voyeuristic psychological thriller with the occasional horror elements (jump scares) that is a must play for horror fans and might be worth checking out on sale for people who like story rich games.  Here is what you need to know:
+Doing all interactions through the phone is very well done.
+Phone UI includes a menu of sorts that shows options of things to do next, and choices you have made.
+All character personalities and writing is well done, but...
-Some of the in-person acting via video seems weak, but part of it could be the inherent awkwardness of characters or their situations.
-The story doesn't seem to really branch out, as it seems more on rails than branching given that choices influence actions that contribute to the end result but don't have a notable impact on the story other than how characters react/feel about you.
-Your in-game surroundings/background and the rare background noises outside of the phone have no relevance to what is actually going on, other than to set a "mood" and randomly have the chance at jump scaring you.  IMO all jump scares should happen within the context of what is ACTUALLY happening, otherwise the other jump scares have faster diminishing returns.
?I don't know that I was compelled enough by the story to want to play through again at 3-4 hours length to get a different ending and see how they interact with me differently.

review_text_raw:
Picture this: you find a girl's phone, and her name is Anna. But here's the catch - she's missing, and you're the one holding her phone with all its personal information. Creepy, right?

The story revolves around investigating Anna's disappearance, and as you interact with her friends and family through text messages and phone conversations, the tension keeps building up. The drama feels real, and the game's decision-based mechanics force you to make choices that affect the outcome. The best part is, it's not just a mystery unraveling over time; your main goal is clear - find Anna. But beware, Simulacra is not just about jumpscares; it plays with your senses more subtly, with eerie audio effects that might even make you question reality outside the game.

Though the game is quite engaging, it's not without its flaws. The voice acting feels a bit awkward and scripted, and some audio elements seem unnecessary, primarily existing for the sake of providing a jumpscare. But hey, the recorded videos are well done, especially Anna's personal vlogs.

Playing this game on PC might not be as immersive as on a mobile phone but it holds its merit reguardless. Still, they could've allowed portrait mode like in Downwell to make it even better.

All in all, Simulacra is a decent horror title that excels in subtle horror and decision-based gameplay. It really makes you think about privacy, honesty, and data security, and that's something you don't often get from a horror game. So, if you're up for an unnerving experience that's a bit different from the usual horror games, give Simulacra a try!

Mostly liked this game.

There were a few good varied 'puzzles' for finding passwords etc, which I liked.

The storyline and dialogue was written so that i was never entirely sure who kidnapped the phone's owner.

On conclusion of the game, it was interesting to see what choices affected the outcome, and used that to try for alt. endings.
After the first completion, the game runs quicker on replay, tho wd have preferred ability to click thru the dialogues instead.
As there are no save points, there is no option but to replay the whole thing for alt. endings and achievements.
It was quicker the second time, due to knowing which files arent necessary to activate or find clues in.

Besides no skip scene options, the gameplay was intuitve and the production was good.
My only peeve was one of the characters. Tho he is supposed to be and ass, and i did get him to apologise to me, on the second run-thru (probably coz i had less patience for his bs) he rrreeealllly iritated me. Being an important character, there is no avoiding him and i just wanted to smack him in the head. So many times I wanted to just 'hang up' on him, tho there isnt that ability, and found myself actually talking back to him, in frustration of what a dick he is. Im all for 'everyone has their own individual paths and reasons for being who and where they are' as in 'you dont put down a baby for not knowing how to spell coz they're a baby' but he is such an ass - his type give men a bad name, ass.
So he is the reason for me mostly liking this game, and why im reluctant to replay for the remaining 9/23 achievements, as well as not being able to skip scenes, particularly towards the end.

If you like these 'Missing Phone Owner' games, and can tolerate a doosh, you will like this game.

TLDR: Cute little horror game with lots of jump scares and some bad acting. Social media in this game was amazing fun. Pick it up on sale.

An adventure horror game all happening in somebody's phone. You essentially play as yourself, trying to solve the mystery of the phone's owner's disappearance with the help of her friends. The puzzles are not very difficult, but engaging enough to keep you hooked in the story. There were some really spooky segments so I'd recommend playing this in a dark quiet room to get its full potential.

The story was fun, reasonably short. Editing Anna's social media was definitely the biggest highlight of my playthrough - you get absolute freedom in Anna's phone. Devs could only make this better by adding more consequences to it. You will spend a lot of time talking to 2 of the biggest cringelords in games everywhere. Their strange behavior was topped off by their atrocious acting. Female acting was alright. There are multiple endings to reflect your choices.

All in all, I recommend getting this one on sale. It's not the best or most memorable game ever, but it's still fairly entertaining..

A refreshingly unique concept for a video game. It does involve a lot of reading but it was usually very well written and hence would usually be very interesting. I am not someone who enjoys games that have too much reading but this game is a surprising exception. 
The concept for the game was so interesting but did they execute it well? Yes, a thousand times yes. So glad I purchased this game and so glad I played it. I played the whole thing in one sitting.

Very well written, your decisions do matter as they have consequences. Some of the characters are very likeable as well.  

You feel like a detective uncovering a mysterious and horrifying story. 
Regarding the horror, it doesnt have too much horror honestly - and some of the horror are just jumpscares. However its not all jumpscares. Some of the horror is due to the story and it's twists and revelations, due to its suspense as you figure out things. 

Massive amount of replayability too, it seems to have several endings depending on your choices.

The ending scenes gave me goosebumps and were genuinely terrifying at times. 

Really well done by the developers, shows they put in a massive amount of thought and work into this, very great product and a completely unique experience. A rare gem.

Well, what can I say? Not at all what I expected from this kind of game. I expected to be a little bored. I expected it to feel repetitive. I expected to quit before the game was over. That's not what happened at all.

For the price it can't be faulted and I would have paid more. The best way to play this is on your mobile phone, but I played the first time on my PC and  found it just as immersive. 

This game will not treat you like a child and it will not hold your hand. You will have to think and you will have to figure things out.

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I’m really shocked how such a “small” yet “simple” game could be such a banger, it is great, interesting and awesome. Full playthrough took me about 6 hours and it was amazing – the gameplay is very simple, you just go through the found smartphone, but it is so fresh and original that you can’t stop diving deeper into the gameplay and story; the story itself is very catchy and it mediates between a cool (and I mean really cool) horror story and kind of detective, where you need to solve smart, interesting puzzles. But here are the important things: it does not feel like just a solving puzzles, you literally investigating a very strange and creepy case, everything feels so alive and real (characters, surfing through the mail, chatting, etc.) and most important that it creates a strong feeling that the choices matter – crazy plot twists, extreme tension, and the sense of realism; about horror –  it’s just perfect, not very much of it but it is placed at the right moments and always hits at the right time. 
It definitely gives me some cool vibes that are crazy mix between “laptop” horror movies (Open Windows, Unfriend) and oldschool “teenager” horrors series (Tales From The Crypt, Are You Afraid Of The Dark?). One of the best games I’ve played for a long time and definitely a hidden gem. 
Do I recommend this game? Strongly recommend.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

review_text_raw:
Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.

review_text_raw:
Fun game for something quite different, a bit like a detective style game using a phone interface to get to the truth.

GOOD STUFF: To me, i enjoyed it for the novelty, and there are different endings for your choices.... They have tried some unique puzzle ideas, you do have to go back and forth through lots of phone based media to solve stuff, and the game often gives you options for hints, if you want them, when stuck instead of just straight delivering them to you after 2 seconds.  They tried to capture how the current world of social media and dating can feel and added some light humour throughout the game.  if you like solving crime style puzzles with a little mystery element added on top, it is worth the short playtime for a bit of fun.

BAD STUFF: However the ridiculous immaturity/selfishness/general mood of ALL the characters had me struggling to want to side with, save or even continue to want to interact with almost any of them as the game went on... It almost makes sense, as they are around 20yrs of age, that they would be a little naive, hot headed, horny and impulsive but yeesh.... waaaaay overboard, none of them ever understand if you do anything for the safety of yourself OR them, and so much of the dialogue has an extreme teen gossip feel, omg he said that you said that she did THAAAAT guurrrrrl im not talking for 2 mins to show I hate you!!! :O haha!  
Similarly the options you can choose between often force you to move the game onwards in a way I would never even consider and would actively steer clear of if I was in this situation.... but I understand it's very difficult to set up enough paths for players to feel like they really have a choice with these things.... Still some work could be done to not feeeeeel like your responses are so forced in a certain direction.  Maybe I missed it too at the start? But suggesting your character is unable to speak or something would help make some of the game moments easier to understand/improve immersion as well.

I really appreciate what the devs have done here, and hope they continue to make some fun games with a difference to the standard algorithm stuff that floods the markets these days. It would be great if they can find a way to let characters adapt to understand the players personality and choices a little more, it's so important to games like this where you are expected to solve a crisis situation if it feels even remotely like it was your actual choices as a person that led to the consequences you get :).

review_text_raw:
[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

Yooooo this game is cool!  Simulacra is my first Kaigan game, so if it cribs from any other games they've made, I wouldn't know yet (I've seen reviews saying this game is similar to others, but I'm fresh to the series/catalog..)  

In my first play-through, I failed hard.. Without spoiling too much, let it suffice to say I didn't save the people I was supposed to save.

Some positives:  The choices in the game actually have some bearing on the outcome of the game.  In my first play-through, I chose to be snarky/sarcastic at times.  My snark made me laugh at the time, but came back to bite me in the end.

I find myself _wanting_ to play again, so I can make better decisions.

Some slight negatives: The acting is a wee bit corny at times, but overall, mostly well-done.  Also, the conversation feels a bit "forced" sometimes.  That happens with games like this -- basically, sometimes, it feels like, no matter what you say, the response you get is the same..  I understand that that's a consequence of having to wrap dialog up, but sometimes the progression can be jarring.  Still, it's only a minor issue. 

To me, this game is not very scary (but I have a pretty high horror threshold, so take what I say with a grain of salt.. I watched the original "It" when I was 7 years old.. then I leaned into the whole horror movie/horror game thing..  I watch horror movies alone, in the dark.. So.. yeah..)

Still, overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  I found the presentation (playing the entire game via the interface of someone else's phone) to be interesting, and I want to play again and figure out how to get more positive endings than the one I got the first time around.

Went into this completely blind and found it to be a decent game with a slightly above average horror storyline. There are a lot of jump-scare tactics in this visual novel/detective game, many of them unnecessary and overused. The FMVs were done pretty well and the interface is intuitive. The game encourages you to play it again to get different outcomes, but when the first playthrough is over 3 hours I can't be bothered to play a linear story and make sure that I selected certain dialogue options to get all endings/100% achievements.

One thing that I absolutely found hilarious was Greg's voice acting. It's so campy and over-the-top that the first time I heard it I couldn't help but bust out laughing. I'm sure that when he recorded it he had to be clear and precise with his lines, but holy crap it just sounds like a Dragonball Z character powering up for a fight.

I recommend this only because what it does well, it does it *really* well (atmosphere, NPC dialogue, FMV, interface). For the other stuff, it's borderline 80's slasher B-movie status trying to take itself a bit too seriously. There seemed to be some missed opportunities here and gaping plot holes, but I would play another game very similar to this by the same developer with a few new tricks.

Overall, mostly worth your time. Might play Simulacra 2 when I get the chance.

I am late as hell but wow, I gotta say it doesn't matter what time you decide to play this game.  If you like Psychological Horror games then this is one to check out.  It's dirt cheap at only 5 bucks (2.24) at the time of this review.  I have always been a fan of investigation games and this one is unique in it's delivery. review_text_raw: Simulacra is a fun, spooky and immersive game where the decisions you make have far-reaching (and unforeseeable) consequences. Multiple endings encourage multiple playthroughs, which is great, but it can be frustrating when the sum of all your choices and hours spent making them lead to complete failure. That's not a negative though! The gameplay is fully fleshed out and it's truly a pleasurable experience regardless of the outcome.  I just finished the first playthrough and I already want to dive back in. If that's not the mark of a great game, I don't know what is.

Also, take my comments on the linearity with a pinch of salt as I have only performed one playthrough, this is just what seems to be the case to me.

The story in general seems ok, but available endings look vagous, and route to them seem to miss some logic steps. It feels like your decisions don't matter at all, since all consequences are some-mysterious-entity left-heel choice. Of course it is scrupulously scripted by devs, but something is missing and "why it ended this way?" question is kept unanswered.

A horror/immersive sim/visual novel game where all you see in front of you is the appearance of a mobile phone. A girl is missing and you have her phone... You meet different people and have to solve things out.
Choices matter, do you make the same choices as others, replayable with multiple endings and various easter eggs (as I read after just completing it). It took me 5 hours to complete and I'd recommend it if you're interested in trying something different.
